name: Dino
baseline: CPython 3.4.x (the same table also lists Ruby 2.1.x, PyPy 2.2.x, JavaScript 1.8.x SpiderMonkey/TraceMonkey, Scala 2.10.x, OCaml 4.0.x; Lua, Duktape and QuickJS are not compared)
workload: Fourteen old shootout-style microbenchmarks (loop, hash, fact, fib, exceptions, methods, objects, sieve, sort, statistics, random, threads, startup, compile) timed on x86-64, AARCH64, ARM and PPC64; every number is a time ratio with the best Dino result (JIT, pure-function and inline hints) as 1.0.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 table, ratios to best Dino = 1.0. Default Dino vs Python: Loop 19 vs 257, Hash 1.0 vs 2.4, Fact 13.2 vs 90.4, Fib 112 vs 492, Except 1.0 vs 9.7, Method 1.0 vs 5.8, Object 1.0 vs 4.4, Sieve 1.0 vs 37.9, Sort 1.4 vs 13.3, Stat 1.0 vs 2.6, Random 3.1 vs 26.9, Thread 1.0 vs 125, Start 1.0 vs 10.9, Compile 1.0 vs 3.3. Default Dino is ahead of Python on all 14 columns (derived from page data). Versus the JS row: JS is faster on Sort (0.6 vs 1.4), Random (0.5 vs 3.1) and Compile (0.8 vs 1.0).
hardware: x86-64: Intel i5-4670 3.4GHz Haswell; AARCH64: X-Gene; ARM: Exynos 5410 1.6GHz Cortex-A15; PPC64: 3.5GHz Power7
tradeoffs: Standalone bytecode interpreter with a C-extern mechanism; the README documents no embedding C API, so using it as an embedded engine from C++ means shelling out or writing glue. Function-level JIT works by invoking a C compiler, which the README itself calls too heavy for some systems. Copyleft licence (GPL-2.0 core). Multi-precision integers and Unicode regexps use GMP and Oniguruma.
caveats: Benchmarks are first-party, 2016-era (document dated Apr 2, 2016) and use CPython 3.4.x, Ruby 2.1.x and PyPy 2.2.x on 2013-era hardware; compiler and flags are not stated. Best-Dino rows use JIT, pure-function and inline hints, so only the plain Dino row is comparable to the other languages' defaults. Dino default loses to PyPy on Hash, Fact, Except, Method, Object, Random and others, and to the JS row on three columns. No comparison against Lua, Duktape or QuickJS exists in the repo; the HN comment that Dino is much faster than Lua could not be opened. Benchmark script is DINO/compare.tst (present in the repo, not read in full). The AARCH64 table used Python 2.7.5 because Python 3 was absent there.

(item 44193355) calling Dino much faster than Lua; threads could not be opened, claim judged from the repo README.

name: QJS (fastschema/qjs)
baseline: goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine) and ModerncQuickJS (modernc.org QuickJS transpiled to Go)
workload: factorial(10) computed 1,000,000 times (5 runs each), plus the AreWeFastYet V8-V7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run from Go.
claimed_speedup: Factorial: QJS 746.132ms average vs GOJA 1.127s (1.51x) and ModerncQuickJS 1.910s (2.56x). V8-V7 score 498 vs GOJA 442 and ModerncQuickJS 323; duration 72.004s vs 78.349s and 97.240s; GOJA wins RegExp (381 vs QJS 142).
tradeoffs: Runs QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly inside the Wazero runtime, so no CGO and a sandbox with memory limits, at the cost of the Wasm layer and a Go-only API. Pre-1.0 (release tags v0.0.1 to v0.0.6 seen on the releases page).
caveats: It is a wrapper of QuickJS, so it probably folds into QuickJS as a duplicate; the baselines are Go engines, and native QuickJS, Lua or Duktape are not benchmarked, so the result says nothing about the C engines. The benchmark code path, Go version and flags are not given in the README. Last commit and release year could not be confirmed (releases page showed dates without a year). The HN link is unconfirmed: the thread title 'Show HN: Pure Go QuickJS JavaScript engine (Golang)' was matched to this project by description only.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com, query 'Show HN small embeddable JavaScript engine faster than QuickJS' returned the thread 'Show HN: Pure Go QuickJS JavaScript engine (Golang)' (item 43962304); the thread could not be opened, and the repo was matched by description (CGO-free QuickJS in Go), not confirmed to be the one posted.

name: Zef
workload: Wall-clock seconds for four scripts (nbody, splay, richards, deltablue) written once per language and run by python3.10, lua 5.4.7, qjs and successive Zef builds; the repo's CSV ends with a geometric-mean row.
claimed_speedup: Geometric-mean seconds in run-benchmarks-results-1776652178.csv: CPython 3.10 0.1296, Lua 0.0577, QuickJS 0.2036, Zef Fil-C++ build (build-21-noasserts) 0.2759, Zef yoloBuild 0.0686. The yoloBuild beats QuickJS on splay (0.3992 vs 0.7090), richards (0.0309 vs 0.7193) and deltablue (0.0784 vs 0.1585) but not nbody (0.0233 vs 0.0214), and beats CPython on all four rows; versus Lua it wins splay (0.3992 vs 0.4393) and deltablue (0.0784 vs 0.0832) and loses nbody and richards. Derived from page data: yoloBuild geomean is about 2.97x faster than QuickJS, 1.89x faster than CPython and 1.19x slower than Lua. The memory-safe Fil-C++ build is slower than all three. The write-up title (snippet only) and the author's post say the 16x speedup brings the AST interpreter to the neighbourhood of CPython, Lua and QuickJS, so parity rather than a win is the author's own claim.
compiler_and_flags: Documented build is Fil-C++ 0.678+ with Meson and Ninja (memory-safe, slower); the faster 'yoloBuild' column uses Yolo-C++ (commit 'Make it possible to build with Yolo-C++', Apr 19 2026); flags not stated.
tradeoffs: AST-walking interpreter (NaN boxing, stack-frame slots, watchpoints, inline caches, no bytecode or JIT); the fast numbers need the memory-unsafe Yolo-C++ build, while the Fil-C++ build the README documents is memory-safe but 4.8x slower than Lua (derived from page data). Standalone interpreter with no documented embedding API; no GC-pause or memory data given.
caveats: Only four benchmarks; CPU model, OS, compiler flags, run counts and spread are not given. The yoloBuild column comes from a differently named build directory (pizlscript/yoloBuild vs pizlscript2) and its exact source revision is not stated. Single-author pre-release language with no LICENSE file found (raw LICENSE returned 404) and the README names no licence, hence reference only. The repo does not claim to be faster than Lua or QuickJS; the win over QuickJS and CPython is read off the CSV. The blog post at zef-lang.dev is blocked here, so its text is known from search snippets only.
